term: "Naive Bayes"

## Simple explanation

Naive Bayes predicts a class by combining how common that class is with how
likely the observed features are under that class. It is called "naive"
because it treats features as conditionally independent given the class,
which is usually an approximation.

## Technical explanation

For class $c$ and features $x_1,\ldots,x_d$, Bayes' rule gives:

$$
P(c \mid x_1,\ldots,x_d)
\propto P(c)\,P(x_1,\ldots,x_d \mid c)
$$

Naive Bayes assumes
$P(x_1,\ldots,x_d \mid c)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}P(x_j \mid c)$.
Variants such as Gaussian, Multinomial, and Bernoulli Naive Bayes model
different kinds of features.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

It trains quickly, scales to high-dimensional sparse data, and provides a
strong baseline for tasks such as spam filtering and text categorization.
Its probability estimates can be poorly calibrated, so scores should not
automatically be treated as reliable confidence.

## How it works

Training estimates class priors and feature likelihoods from labeled
examples. At prediction time, the model computes a score for each class and
selects the largest. Implementations commonly use log probabilities to
avoid numerical underflow:

$$
\log P(c \mid x) \propto \log P(c) + \sum_j \log P(x_j \mid c)
$$

## Practical example

In a word-based spam filter, Multinomial Naive Bayes estimates how often
each word occurs in spam and non-spam messages. The words in a new email
update the two class scores, and the larger score determines the predicted
label.

## Common misconceptions

- Conditional independence is an assumption of the model, not a claim that real-world features are independent.
- "Naive" does not mean useless; the approximation can work well for some tasks.
- A high class score is not necessarily a calibrated probability.
